nameStory: This cheerful wildflower gets its whimsical name from its unusual seed pods, which split into several curved sections that look remarkably like tiny bird feet! The 'trefoil' part refers to its three-leaflet leaves, though it actually has five leaflets per leaf. Some folks call it 'eggs and bacon' because of its bright yellow petals often tinged with orange or red.
description: Bird's-foot trefoil is a low-growing perennial wildflower that spreads along the ground or forms small mounds up to about a foot tall. It's covered in bright yellow pea-like flowers from late spring through fall, creating cheerful golden patches in fields and roadsides. The plant belongs to the legume family, so it's related to peas and beans, and has the characteristic compound leaves with small oval leaflets. Originally from Europe, it's now naturalized throughout New England and valued as livestock feed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow pea-shaped flowers about half an inch long, often with orange or reddish streaks on the back petals. They cluster in groups of 3-8 flowers at the tips of stems and feel papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Each leaf has 5 oval leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand - 3 at the tip and 2 lower down that look like tiny green thumbs. The leaflets feel smooth and slightly thick, with a subtle sweet smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive brown seed pods that split into 4-6 curved, claw-like segments resembling bird feet. The pods are about an inch long and make a subtle rattling sound when dry and shaken.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mats or trailing patches, rarely over 12 inches tall. Stems are hollow and can root at joints where they touch the ground, creating expanding colonies.

habitat: Look for bird's-foot trefoil in sunny, open areas like fields, meadows, roadsides, and disturbed soils throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained soils and is particularly common along highway edges and in agricultural areas. This adaptable plant tolerates poor soils and drought once established.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge in early spring, with the first bright yellow flowers appearing in late May. Young leaves are tender and the most vibrant green of the year.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant yellow flowers from June through August. Plants are at their most robust, forming dense mats in suitable habitat.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into early fall while distinctive bird-foot seed pods mature and split open. Leaves may turn yellowish but often stay green until frost.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to the ground, leaving dried stems and scattered seed pods. Look for small rosettes of leaves that may persist in mild winters under snow.

funFact: Bird's-foot trefoil is like a natural fertilizer factory - it partners with special bacteria in root nodules to capture nitrogen from the air and convert it into plant food, actually improving the soil for other plants around it!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with wild clover, but bird's-foot trefoil has 5 leaflets per leaf (not 3 like clover) and yellow flowers (not white or pink). Remember: 'Five fingers, yellow flowers' for bird's-foot trefoil versus 'three leaves, white or pink' for clover.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'trefoil' (meaning three-leaved), this plant actually has five leaflets per leaf, which can confuse beginners. The name stuck from older botanical traditions when the two lower leaflets were considered separate structures called stipules.
compareHints: Bird's-foot trefoil is much more common than its relatives narrow-leaf bird's-foot trefoil and greater bird's-foot trefoil in New England. The narrow-leaf species has much thinner, almost grass-like leaflets, while the greater species is taller and prefers wetter soils. Common bird's-foot trefoil has the broadest leaflets and most robust flowers of the three.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to regular bird's-foot trefoil, this species is much more delicate with narrower leaves, thinner stems, and smaller flowers.
Greater bird's-foot trefoil is the giant of the bird's-foot trefoil family, significantly larger and more robust than both regular bird's-foot trefoil and narrow-leaf bird's-foot trefoil.
